analysis.data_caveats: A substantial share of "conflict" and "political_violence_targeting_civilians" events in this window are GDELT-derived items that appear to be miscoded or off-topic (e.g., US Supreme Court/TPS coverage, JD Vance opinion pieces, a "ROCKEFELLER FOUNDATION" fighting event, a West Virginia relief story) rather than verified on-the-ground Haiti incidents — these should be treated with low confidence and are not corroborated by ACLED-style ground reporting. Investment data is heavily skewed toward historical (2010-2019) Chinese soft-diplomacy grants/scholarships and a few DFC/PPI deals, with no recorded investment activity after 2019, making recent financing trends unobservable. Only 3 events are tagged specifically "protest_civil_unrest," so unrest-pattern conclusions rely heavily on the conflict/political-violence categories, which are themselves of mixed reliability.
analysis.economic_analysis: IMF data shows Haiti's economy contracting for a second consecutive year: real GDP growth of -2.7% in 2025 and a projected -1.7% in 2026 (IMF), consistent with World Bank's -2.7% GDP growth figure for 2025. Inflation remains very high, at 28.3% (IMF, 2025) / 28.6% (World Bank, 2025), moderating only slightly to a projected 23.5% average for 2026 (IMF). Government gross debt is comparatively low and falling (12.3% of GDP in 2025 to 10.7% in 2026, IMF), and the current account is near balance (1.9% of GDP in 2025 narrowing to 0.2% in 2026, IMF), but unemployment sits at 14.9% (World Bank, 2025) and FDI inflows are negligible at just 0.1% of GDP (World Bank, 2024), alongside a modest external debt stock of $944.7M (World Bank, 2024). The combination of recession, high inflation, high unemployment, and near-zero FDI signals a macroeconomic environment under sustained stress despite low sovereign debt levels.
analysis.investment_analysis: Recorded investment activity is dominated by the "Unspecified Chinese Government Institution" actor (32 of 45 investment events), consisting primarily of education/scholarship grants, undisclosed-value donations (school supplies, sporting goods, office equipment), and two large unfulfilled pledges: a $1.2B MoU for an electrical grid (AidData, 2016-10-14) and an $800M MoU for an agriculture project (AidData, 2015-01-01), both still listed as "Pipeline: Pledge" with no recorded follow-through or disbursement events since. US-linked private/DFC financing is comparatively small — a $19.5M direct loan to the Marriott Autograph Collection hotel (DFC, FY2019), a $1.5M unfunded guaranty to MCE Social Capital and a $1.0M unfunded guaranty to Sogebank (DFC, FY2015). World Bank PPI records show two greenfield private infrastructure projects: Port Lafito ($57.2M, seaports, active since 2014) and NatCom (telecom, active since 2011). No investment events are recorded after 2019, indicating either a data gap or a sharp pullback in traceable formal development-finance/private investment activity in the last several years.
analysis.security_analysis: The conflict data for the 2026-07-01/02 window is dominated by items of questionable Haiti-relevance sourced from GDELT (e.g., a "CONGRESS <-> PRESIDENT" fighting item tied to a US Supreme Court story, and a "ROCKEFELLER FOUNDATION" fighting item tied to a Forbes electrification piece), alongside more plausible Haiti-specific signals: an "ARMED GANG <-> PORT AU PRINCE" conflict entry and a "POPULATION <-> GANG" entry both sourced to the Security Council Report's July 2026 Haiti monthly forecast (securitycouncilreport.org, 2026-07-01), and a "LOCAL MEDIA <-> POLICE" coercion event tied to the medical-student hospital-relocation protest (africanews.com, 2026-07-02). Severity scores for these events cluster very high (7.7–9.5), but none carry fatality figures, limiting the ability to gauge lethality. The presence of gang-population conflict entries corroborated by the UN Security Council's monthly Haiti forecast is the most credible security signal in this dataset, pointing to continued armed-gang control/contestation in Port-au-Prince.
analysis.political_stability_analysis: Civil unrest signals are thin (only 3 tagged protest_civil_unrest events), the clearest being a medical-student protest demanding relocation of a Port-au-Prince teaching hospital, alongside fighting at the hospital itself and coercion of local media by police (all africanews.com, 2026-07-02). Several "political_violence_targeting_civilians" entries reference an "ADMINISTRATION <-> IMMIGRANT" and "unspecified actor <-> PRESIDENT" dynamic (GDELT, 2026-06-30/07-01) tied to US TPS/immigration policy coverage (Jamaica Observer, Yahoo News) rather than domestic Haitian civilian-targeting violence, suggesting these are largely diaspora/US-policy stories swept into the Haiti dataset rather than direct evidence of political violence inside Haiti. The most Haiti-grounded stability signal is the gang-population conflict noted in the Security Council Report (2026-07-01), consistent with continued non-state armed-actor pressure on civilians in the capital.
analysis.trend_summary: The data presents a fragile macroeconomic picture (contracting GDP, high inflation, high unemployment) combined with a security/political dataset that is heavily diluted by apparently miscategorized GDELT items referencing US domestic politics and immigration policy rather than Haiti-specific events. The most credible domestic signals point to continued gang control/violence in Port-au-Prince (Security Council Report, 2026-07-01) and localized civil unrest around public services (medical student protest over hospital relocation, africanews.com, 2026-07-02). Investment/development-finance activity shows a long history of Chinese grants and soft-diplomacy engagement plus large unfulfilled infrastructure pledges, but no recorded new investment activity since 2019, alongside near-zero FDI inflows (World Bank, 2024). Overall the pattern is one of macroeconomic contraction, thin and low-confidence security data, sparse recent formal investment, and heavy entanglement of the dataset with US-focused immigration/TPS narratives concerning Haitian nationals.
key_relationships: - Security Council Report's July 2026 Haiti monthly forecast is the source for both an "ARMED GANG <-> PORT AU PRINCE" and "POPULATION <-> GANG" conflict entry (2026-07-01), the most credible gang-violence signal in the dataset.

- Medical students, government, and police intersect around a hospital-relocation demand in Port-au-Prince, with associated fighting-at-hospital and police-media coercion events, all dated 2026-07-02 (africanews.com/GDELT).

- China ("Unspecified Chinese Government Institution") is the dominant investment actor (32 of 45 investment events), spanning education grants, equipment donations, and two large unfulfilled pledges: a $1.2B energy-grid MoU (AidData, 2016-10-14) and an $800M agriculture MoU (AidData, 2015-01-01).

- US-linked actors appear across conflict, political-violence, and humanitarian categories (20 events), frequently tied to US TPS/immigration policy stories (Yahoo News, 2026-07-01; Jamaica Observer, 2026-06-29) rather than in-country Haiti events.

- DFC financed a $19.5M hotel project (Marriott Autograph Collection, FY2019) and small guaranties to Sogebank and MCE Social Capital (FY2015), while World Bank PPI lists Port Lafito ($57.2M seaport, active 2014) and NatCom (telecom, active 2011) as ongoing private infrastructure projects.
risk_flags: - Two large Chinese infrastructure pledges ($1.2B energy grid, 2016; $800M agriculture project, 2015, both AidData) remain at "Pipeline: Pledge" status with no recorded disbursement or completion events, suggesting stalled follow-through.

- No investment/development-finance events recorded after 2019, versus a recession recorded through 2026 (IMF/World Bank), indicating a possible financing gap or data blind spot during the deepest downturn.
- FDI net inflows at just 0.1% of GDP (World Bank, 2024) alongside contracting GDP (-2.7% in 2025, -1.7% projected 2026, IMF) point to weak external capital formation.
- Gang-population conflict corroborated by the UN Security Council Report (2026-07-01) indicates continued non-state armed control in Port-au-Prince, a direct operating-environment risk.

- A large share of "conflict" and "political_violence_targeting_civilians" tagged events (e.g., 2026-07-01/02 GDELT items referencing US Congress, Supreme Court, JD Vance, Rockefeller Foundation) appear to be data-quality/miscategorization issues rather than genuine Haiti security incidents, warranting caution in any automated severity scoring.
